PR8-F-01.hint: Find where the quadratic equals zero. Those numbers split the number line into intervals; test one point in each interval to see where the inequality is true.
slips: Using brackets for a strict inequality, or parentheses when the inequality includes equality.
Writing \(x<a\) and \(x>b\) as one interval. When the solution is the outside, you need two intervals joined with \(\cup\).

PR8-A-01.hint: Get zero on one side first. If the quadratic never crosses the \(x\)-axis, the answer is either every real number or no real number, depending on the inequality.
slips: Dividing or moving terms and forgetting to reverse the inequality when you multiply or divide by a negative number.
Reporting an interval when the quadratic has no real zeros. Check the discriminant first.

parts.q: Solve \(x^{2} - 36 \gt  0\). Express your answer in interval notation.
parts.a: Solve \(x^{2} - 36 = 0\): \(x = -6\) and \(x = 6\). These split the number line into three intervals. Test a point in each interval to see where \(x^{2} - 36 \gt  0\) is true. The endpoints are not included because the inequality is strict. Solution: \((-\infty, -6) \cup (6, \infty)\).

parts.q: Solve \(2 x^{2} + 6 x \ge 8\). Express your answer in interval notation.
parts.a: Subtract \(8\) from both sides to get \(2 x^{2} + 6 x - 8 \ge 0\), then factor and use a sign chart. Solution: \((-\infty, -4] \cup [1, \infty)\).

parts.q: Solve \(x^{2} - 6 x + 12 \ge 0\). Express your answer in interval notation, or say there is no real solution.
parts.a: The discriminant is \(b^2 - 4ac = -12\), which is negative, so the parabola never touches the \(x\)-axis. It opens upward, so \(x^{2} - 6 x + 12\) is always positive. Therefore every real number is a solution: \((-\infty, \infty)\).
